symptom: ako/mxcli#2094 (mendixlabs/mxcli#1795): on a large MPR v1 project exec took 0.3 s per `create microflow` and 0.9 s per one-activity `create or modify`, check 0.5 s per statement, whatever the statement changed; the cost was fixed per statement, not growing with the run, and v2 projects of similar shape were an order of magnitude cheaper.
cause: listUnitsByTypeV1In rescanned the metadata of the whole Unit table on every typed listing to revalidate its type index (v1 updateUnit did not invalidate, so the scan was the only change detector), and a statement makes dozens of listings; ListUnitHeaders on v1 read the full contents of every unit of the type to get the names, so each lookup by name read every microflow.
file: modelsdk/mpr/reader_units_v1.go (unitMetasV1 + v1Stamp keep the scan; listUnitHeadersV1 keeps Name/Excluded by length + ContentsHash), modelsdk/mpr/reader_units.go (InvalidateCache reaches it; ListUnitHeaders v1 path), modelsdk/mpr/writer_core.go (v1 updateUnit invalidates like every other write)
insight: Profile before guessing: a CPU profile of 50 statements put 54% in listUnitsByTypeV1 and showed exec's preflight doing the same planning first. The reader holds ONE SQLite connection (SetMaxOpenConns(1)), which makes PRAGMA data_version an exact detector for commits by any other connection or process — its own writes do not move it, so they invalidate explicitly; file size+mtime is only a second signal, because on Windows they can lag for an open file. A unit's $Type is fixed for life but its Name is not, so names are keyed on length AND ContentsHash, and a foreign commit drops them all since nothing obliges another writer to set the hash. Test with the file-stat signal off (reader path empty), or the stat masks a missing invalidation. Measured on OneHarness (3,400 units): create 0.30 -> 0.11 s, create or modify 0.86 -> 0.35 s, check of 150 statements 76 -> 15 s. What remains is backend-level: ListDomainModels and ListMicroflows decode every unit per call, and the preflight plans each flow change twice.
